claims.claim: Le Guin holds that style is not an ingredient added to a fantasy but the book itself; strip it and only a plot synopsis remains, a claim she calls 'absolutely true of fantasy'.
claims.source: Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1973), full essay text (PDF)
claims.quote: The style, of course, is the book.

claims.claim: She argues most epics, the Mabinogion and the sagas use straightforward language that keeps oral directness, and that plainness is the noblest and hardest register for heroic fantasy.
claims.source: Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1973), full essay text (PDF)
claims.quote: A plain language is the noblest of all.

claims.claim: She separates true plainness from the flat, inexact 'Poughkeepsie' prose of commercial fantasy, which is journalism's deliberate suppression of sensibility applied to the remote and elemental.
claims.source: Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1973), full essay text (PDF)
claims.quote: It is not really simple, but flat.

claims.claim: Sensory cues are 'extremely important in imaginative writing'; when rocks, wind and trees are vague and generalized the scene is not felt.
claims.source: Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1973), full essay text (PDF)
claims.quote: the scenery is cardboard, or plastic

claims.claim: The archaic manner is a perfect distancer only when done perfectly; botched thee/thou verbs, subjunctives, 'mayhap' and 'ichor' are the touchstones of failure.
claims.source: Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1973), full essay text (PDF)
claims.quote: It's a high wire: one slip spoils all.

claims.claim: Archaisms are inessential to distancing from the ordinary: Jack Vance's aloof, restrained, consistent narrative and dialogue prose is an achieved style with none.
claims.source: Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1973), full essay text (PDF)
claims.quote: And it contains no archaisms at all.

claims.claim: Alternating colloquial American for humour with formal usage for earnest moments (Leiber, Zelazny) jerks the reader between Elfland and Poughkeepsie and dissolves the characters' coherence.
claims.source: Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1973), full essay text (PDF)
claims.quote: the characters lose coherence in my mind

claims.claim: Speech reveals character whether the author knows it or not; a lord who says 'I could have told you that' can never be a hero, and genuine Elfland dialogue cannot be relocated to Capitol Hill by changing four words.
claims.source: Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1973), full essay text (PDF)
claims.quote: Speech expresses character.

claims.claim: Tolkien's plain clear English is praised for flexibility and variety, moving from commonplace to stately and sliding into metre unnoticed, with an unremarkable vocabulary and everything direct, concrete and simple.
claims.source: Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1973), full essay text (PDF)
claims.quote: Its outstanding virtue is its flexibility, its variety.

claims.claim: Good prose, even archaic (Eddison), is judged visually for precision and musically for the sound of words, the movement of syntax and the rhythm of sentences, with nothing faked or blurred.
claims.source: Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1973), full essay text (PDF)
claims.quote: the movement of the syntax, and the rhythm of the sentences

claims.claim: In fantasy there is no borrowed reality to hide flaws, only a construct built in a void with every seam exposed, so every word counts and the only voice is the creator's.
claims.source: Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1973), full essay text (PDF)
claims.quote: And every word counts.

claims.claim: Imitation Dunsany is diagnosed as elaborate made-up names, vague gorgeous cities and many sentences beginning with 'And' — biblical cadence worn as costume.
claims.source: Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1973), full essay text (PDF)
claims.quote: a great many sentences beginning with "And."

claims.claim: The Eddison and Morris dialogue passages show nothing happening (reading a book, dividing a rabbit) yet invest trivial acts with importance, emotion and vitality — the elevation lies in the speech, not the event.
claims.source: Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1973), full essay text (PDF)
claims.quote: with what importance they invest these trivial acts

claims.claim: Tolkien's speakers use 'an English extraordinary for its simple timelessness' with sobriety, wit and force — the language of men of character rather than mannered archaism.
claims.source: Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1973), full essay text (PDF)
claims.quote: an English extraordinary for its simple timelessness

claims.claim: The Wikipedia synthesis reads the essay as claiming fantastic creation must reach into words and grammar, and cites Peter S. Beagle calling it the definitive piece on why sprinkling thees and thous fails.
claims.source: Wikipedia: From Elfland to Poughkeepsie
claims.quote: reach to the very words and grammar

claims.claim: The article lists Dunsany, Eddison, Kenneth Morris, Tolkien, Cabell, Evangeline Walton and Jack Vance as the essay's models of style that fits its world.
claims.source: Wikipedia: From Elfland to Poughkeepsie

claims.claim: Le Guin said fantasy must be clear and direct with language because the reader has no known framework to rest on.
claims.source: Wikipedia: A Wizard of Earthsea (citing Le Guin)
claims.quote: there is no known framework for the reader's mind

claims.claim: Mike Cadden characterizes the Earthsea narration as free indirect discourse in which the protagonist's feelings blend with the narrator's, creating sympathy while keeping narrative flexibility.
claims.source: Wikipedia: A Wizard of Earthsea (citing Cadden, Beyond Genre)
claims.quote: free indirect discourse

claims.claim: The narration assumes the reader already knows Earthsea's geography and history, avoiding heavy exposition, and moves between looking ahead into Ged's future and back into Earthsea's past.
claims.source: Wikipedia: A Wizard of Earthsea
claims.quote: switches from looking ahead into Ged's future

claims.claim: A reviewer credits this method with giving the world Tolkien's mysterious depths 'without his tiresome back-stories'.
claims.source: Wikipedia: A Wizard of Earthsea (citing Amanda Craig)
claims.quote: without his tiresome back-stories

claims.claim: George Slusser described the book's mood as strange and dreamlike, fluctuating between objective reality and Ged's inner thoughts.
claims.source: Wikipedia: A Wizard of Earthsea (citing Slusser 1976)
claims.quote: strange and dreamlike

claims.claim: Amanda Craig (Guardian) praised prose 'as taut and clean as a ship's sail'.
claims.source: Wikipedia: A Wizard of Earthsea (citing Craig)
claims.quote: prose as taut and clean as a ship's sail

claims.claim: Slusser (1976) called the Earthsea cycle a work of high style and imagination with genuine epic vision.
claims.source: Wikipedia: A Wizard of Earthsea (citing Slusser)
claims.quote: work of high style and imagination

claims.claim: Harold Bloom called Le Guin an exquisite stylist with every word exactly in place and every sentence resonant.
claims.source: Wikipedia: Ursula K. Le Guin (citing Bloom)
claims.quote: Every word was exactly in place

claims.claim: The New York Times characterized her prose as a lean but lyrical style used to explore moral issues.
claims.source: Wikipedia: Ursula K. Le Guin (citing NYT)
claims.quote: lean but lyrical style

claims.claim: Zadie Smith called her prose as elegant and beautiful as any written in the twentieth century.
claims.source: Wikipedia: Ursula K. Le Guin (citing Zadie Smith)
claims.quote: as elegant and beautiful as any written

claims.claim: The Left Hand of Darkness is assembled from ethnological reports, myths, diary entries and personal narration, a structure called distinctly post-modern.
claims.source: Wikipedia: Ursula K. Le Guin
claims.quote: distinctly post-modern

claims.claim: Bloom described the Left Hand prose as precise, dialectical and always evocative in its restrained pathos.
claims.source: Wikipedia: The Left Hand of Darkness (citing Bloom)
claims.quote: precise, dialectical—always evocative in its restrained pathos

claims.claim: Gethenian myths and legends are placed before chapters in which Genly Ai meets similar situations, so the embedded texts explain both cultural detail and philosophy.
claims.source: Wikipedia: The Left Hand of Darkness

claims.claim: Ai's first-person report reflects a gradually evolving worldview so the reader's understanding develops with his; the structure was initially found confusing by reviewers (Donna White).
claims.source: Wikipedia: The Left Hand of Darkness (citing White)

claims.claim: Much of Tombs unfolds from Tenar's perspective, the reader feeling the undertomb's fear through her eyes; Cadden's free indirect discourse makes the narrator seem sympathetic to the characters.
claims.source: Wikipedia: The Tombs of Atuan (citing Cadden)
claims.quote: the narrator seem sympathetic to the characters

claims.claim: Jo Walton credits the final travel section with grounding the narrative after the earthquake, 'solid and well rooted as ever'.
claims.source: Wikipedia: The Tombs of Atuan (citing Walton)
claims.quote: solid and well rooted as ever

claims.claim: Kirkus praised Tehanu's flawless, poetic prose and its thoughtful, potent metaphor.
claims.source: Wikipedia: Tehanu (citing Kirkus)
claims.quote: flawless, poetic prose

claims.claim: Michael Dirda found Tehanu less sheerly exciting but perhaps the most moving, with a darker, more realistic edge and a woman's point of view.
claims.source: Wikipedia: Tehanu (citing Dirda)
claims.quote: a darker, more realistic edge

claims.claim: Jo Walton calls Tehanu a restless book with very strange pacing, torn between plot and women's domestic lives.
claims.source: Wikipedia: Tehanu (citing Walton)
claims.quote: a restless book with very strange pacing

claims.feature: plain strong exact diction; grave formal tone
claims.claim: The guide characterizes the language as plain, strong and exact, the tone grave and slightly formal.
claims.source: NEA Big Read Reader's Guide: A Wizard of Earthsea (PDF)
claims.quote: plain, strong, and exact

claims.claim: The rhythm of her sentences is described as carefully balanced and musical.
claims.source: NEA Big Read Reader's Guide: A Wizard of Earthsea (PDF)
claims.quote: carefully balanced and musical

claims.claim: It notes occasional alliteration and assonance reminiscent of Old English verse, citing 'Forest rises ridge behind ridge to the stone and snow of the heights'.
claims.source: NEA Big Read Reader's Guide: A Wizard of Earthsea (PDF)
claims.quote: reminiscent of Old English verse

claims.claim: Le Guin (2008 interview): what a wizard does is like what a writer does — making things out of words and making things happen with words.
claims.source: NEA Big Read Reader's Guide: A Wizard of Earthsea (PDF)
claims.quote: He or she is making things out of words

claims.claim: The guide says The Left Hand of Darkness is written in a tone even more gravely austere than A Wizard of Earthsea.
claims.source: NEA Big Read Reader's Guide: A Wizard of Earthsea (PDF)
claims.quote: a tone even more gravely austere

claims.claim: A discussion question calls the novel's language 'often quietly poetic'.
claims.source: NEA Big Read Reader's Guide: A Wizard of Earthsea (PDF)
claims.quote: often quietly poetic

claims.claim: The introduction credits the book's elegant diction, geographical sweep and mounting suspense.
claims.source: NEA Big Read Reader's Guide: A Wizard of Earthsea (PDF)
claims.quote: elegant diction, geographical sweep, and mounting suspense

claims.claim: The NEA Big Read web page repeats the guide's 'plain, strong, and exact' characterization and pairs it with Craig's 'taut and clean as a ship's sail'.
claims.source: NEA Big Read: A Wizard of Earthsea (web page)
claims.quote: plain, strong, and exact

claims.claim: The SFE calls the initial Earthsea trilogy austere but vivid, a major work reaching beyond its Young Adult audience.
claims.source: Encyclopedia of Science Fiction (SFE), entry 'Le Guin, Ursula K'
claims.quote: austere but vivid

claims.claim: The SFE says a grave joyfulness pervades the trilogy, more maturely thoughtful than Narnia while remaining exciting.
claims.source: Encyclopedia of Science Fiction (SFE), entry 'Le Guin, Ursula K'
claims.quote: A grave joyfulness pervades the trilogy

claims.claim: The Left Hand of Darkness is told in a prose notable for its clarity and evocative precision.
claims.source: Encyclopedia of Science Fiction (SFE), entry 'Le Guin, Ursula K'
claims.quote: a prose notable for its clarity and evocative precision

claims.claim: Archetypal motif pairs (darkness/light, root/branch, language/silence) are woven until the motifs are the story, treated as balanced twins rather than polarities.
claims.source: Encyclopedia of Science Fiction (SFE), entry 'Le Guin, Ursula K'
claims.quote: the motifs are the story

claims.claim: Searoad's nonfantastic stories convey 'the same capably restrained immanence' — restraint named as a constant of her manner.
claims.source: Encyclopedia of Science Fiction (SFE), entry 'Le Guin, Ursula K'
claims.quote: capably restrained immanence

claims.claim: Tehanu is described as a sad, powerful, quiet book about the strength of women.
claims.source: Encyclopedia of Science Fiction (SFE), entry 'Le Guin, Ursula K'
claims.quote: a sad, powerful, quiet book

claims.claim: Le Guin avoids 'magician' (tainted by stage illusion) and coins Archmage, magelight, magewind and magery from Latin magus — none in the OED — so that the vocabulary itself resets the reader's assumptions about magic.
claims.source: Tom Shippey, 'The Magic Art and the Evolution of Words' (Hard Reading, Liverpool UP 2016; orig. Mosaic 1977) — chapter abstract
claims.quote: based on a semantic point

claims.claim: The magic system rests on a 'Rumpelstiltskin theory' in which every thing has a true name distinct from ordinary language, and knowing it gives power — a linguistic premise that carries plot and theme.
claims.source: Tom Shippey, 'The Magic Art and the Evolution of Words' (Hard Reading, Liverpool UP 2016; orig. Mosaic 1977) — chapter abstract
claims.quote: Rumpelstiltskin theory

claims.claim: Kelso reads the Lathe of Heaven jellyfish sentence's four opposing blocks (two compound adjectives, two clauses) as an ocean-on-beach here-and-back rhythm that foreshadows the novel's yin/yang structure of recurrence.
claims.source: Sylvia A. Kelso, 'Boldly to Re-Venture: New Writing on the Works of Ursula K. Le Guin', Paradoxa 21 (2008), pp. 7–22 (PDF)
claims.quote: rhythm at sentence level foreshadows the tenor

claims.claim: Like Yeats, Le Guin moves toward simplicity or austerity in both rhythm and content of later work; Tehanu begins in farm life and ends among a few goats and bean vines.
claims.source: Sylvia A. Kelso, 'Boldly to Re-Venture: New Writing on the Works of Ursula K. Le Guin', Paradoxa 21 (2008), pp. 7–22 (PDF)
claims.quote: move toward simplicity, or at least austerity

claims.claim: In the Tenar–Moss rush-splitting scene the 'business' works as a suite of variations for pause and emphasis: the leisurely 'They split rushes for a while in silence' quickens to the snaps of 'neatly, quickly, with her nail' and is cut by the bare 'They split rushes.'
claims.source: Sylvia A. Kelso, 'Boldly to Re-Venture: New Writing on the Works of Ursula K. Le Guin', Paradoxa 21 (2008), pp. 7–22 (PDF)
claims.quote: a suite of variations to indicate pause and emphasis

claims.feature: long smooth sentence, triple repetition, assonance
claims.claim: Kalessin's arrival pairs an extraordinarily long comma-weighted sentence (weighting 'sinuous', 'claws', 'fire') with a classic triple repetition whose final word links by assonance to the previous paragraph, approaching actual poetry.
claims.source: Sylvia A. Kelso, 'Boldly to Re-Venture: New Writing on the Works of Ursula K. Le Guin', Paradoxa 21 (2008), pp. 7–22 (PDF)
claims.quote: almost somnambulistically smooth

claims.claim: Kelso quotes Le Guin ('Collectors, Rhymesters and Drummers'): holding to the rhythm of the dragon's flight let Tehanu tell itself, and when she lost the beat she fell off and had to wait.
claims.source: Sylvia A. Kelso, 'Boldly to Re-Venture: New Writing on the Works of Ursula K. Le Guin', Paradoxa 21 (2008), pp. 7–22 (PDF)
claims.quote: the very large, long wingbeats

claims.claim: Rhythm analysis slides into vocabulary, 'rhythm's Siamese twin': Lathe's 'tugged hugely' and 'tidal abyss' lean embroidered, while elsewhere the same book reaches a homely simile of love made like bread.
claims.source: Sylvia A. Kelso, 'Boldly to Re-Venture: New Writing on the Works of Ursula K. Le Guin', Paradoxa 21 (2008), pp. 7–22 (PDF)
claims.quote: rhythm's Siamese twin

claims.claim: Tehanu shows 'the skill of experience making less do more, rather than more do more' — the late style compresses.
claims.source: Sylvia A. Kelso, 'Boldly to Re-Venture: New Writing on the Works of Ursula K. Le Guin', Paradoxa 21 (2008), pp. 7–22 (PDF)
claims.quote: making less do more

claims.claim: The Language of the Night established Le Guin's lyrical, unruly and individual critical voice with 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' among its essays.
claims.source: Sylvia A. Kelso, 'Boldly to Re-Venture: New Writing on the Works of Ursula K. Le Guin', Paradoxa 21 (2008), pp. 7–22 (PDF)
claims.quote: lyrical, unruly, and individual critical voice

claims.claim: In the Always Coming Home vision paragraph, a long opening clause checks into shortening phrases, brakes at a colon, then returns through a triple of lengthening units to a singing polysyllable ('over the Obsidian').
claims.source: Sylvia A. Kelso, 'Boldly to Re-Venture: New Writing on the Works of Ursula K. Le Guin', Paradoxa 21 (2008), pp. 7–22 (PDF)
claims.quote: Here there are no rhythmic superfluities.

claims.claim: Le Guin (quoted by Garth) said there was no use trying to make a lexicon of Earthsea's languages, unlike Tolkien who in one sense wrote LOTR to give his languages speakers.
claims.source: John Garth, 'Ursula Le Guin, the language of Earthsea, and Tolkien' (blog)
claims.quote: No use trying to make a lexicon

claims.claim: Attebery (quoted by Garth) distinguishes her from Tolkien copyists as one who absorbed Tolkien, comprehended him and went her own direction.
claims.source: John Garth blog (citing Attebery)
claims.quote: absorbed Tolkien, comprehended him, and gone on in her own direction

claims.claim: Garth notes Le Guin called language invention 'the Secret Vice' after Tolkien's essay and counted LOTR among the three books she had re-read past counting.
claims.source: John Garth blog

claims.claim: In 'Dreams Must Explain Themselves' Le Guin named only the Shorter Oxford Dictionary and Follett's and Fowler's usage manuals as her tools (later Strunk & White).
claims.source: Stan Carey, 'How to see one's own world': Le Guin on writing style (Sentence first blog)
claims.quote: Follett's and Fowler's manuals

claims.claim: Carey foregrounds the essay's claim that style is the writer's way of seeing and speaking, and that the artist's hardest lesson is to see his own world and speak in his own words.
claims.source: Stan Carey blog (quoting Elfland)

claims.claim: Margaret Mahy: in Earthsea language is not only the vehicle of the story but at times what the story is about, and Le Guin must find the right name before she can go on.
claims.source: Margaret Mahy, 'Speculations on the Earthsea Stories' (ursulakleguin.com)
claims.quote: what the story is about

claims.claim: The invented names carry conviction and inevitability, so the reader feels reminded of a land already known.
claims.source: Margaret Mahy (ursulakleguin.com)
claims.quote: conviction and inevitability

claims.feature: spoken voice in the reader's head
claims.claim: Mahy describes the reading experience as words on the page becoming a spoken voice in the reader's head — the storyteller addressing a reader-listener.
claims.source: Margaret Mahy (ursulakleguin.com)
claims.quote: a spoken voice in the reader's head

claims.claim: Walton calls it one of the very few fantasy novels that succeeds in feeling like a legend.
claims.source: Jo Walton, '"Bright the hawk's flight in the empty sky": Ursula Le Guin's A Wizard of Earthsea' (Reactor, 2010)
claims.quote: succeeds in feeling like a legend

claims.claim: The narration passes easily from what people say and what isn't spoken of, from the distance of the fairy-tale teller to the very close, always sure where the teller stands.
claims.source: Jo Walton, '"Bright the hawk's flight in the empty sky": Ursula Le Guin's A Wizard of Earthsea' (Reactor, 2010)
claims.quote: the distance of the teller of fairy-tales to the very close

claims.feature: told within the world, after the story
claims.claim: The story is told entirely within the world but after it, so the implied reader is assumed to know the great deeds referenced.
claims.source: Jo Walton, '"Bright the hawk's flight in the empty sky": Ursula Le Guin's A Wizard of Earthsea' (Reactor, 2010)
claims.quote: told entirely within the world, but after the story

claims.claim: There is never a wasted word and all the words are right; it is like poetry and among the best books for reading aloud.
claims.source: Jo Walton, '"Bright the hawk's flight in the empty sky": Ursula Le Guin's A Wizard of Earthsea' (Reactor, 2010)
claims.quote: There's never a wasted word, and all the words are right.

claims.claim: The names (Selidor, Iffish, Havnor, Osskil, Gont, Pendor) make the map memorable; the world is 'named and called up' from the first word.
claims.source: Jo Walton, '"Bright the hawk's flight in the empty sky": Ursula Le Guin's A Wizard of Earthsea' (Reactor, 2010)
claims.quote: Le Guin is so wonderful with names

claims.claim: A world with much more in it than appears on the page — history, other countries — yet with a clear line drawn round it: 'only in silence the word'.
claims.source: Jo Walton, '"Bright the hawk's flight in the empty sky": Ursula Le Guin's A Wizard of Earthsea' (Reactor, 2010)
claims.quote: a clear line drawn around it

claims.claim: Plotz (per Burt) calls the prose the antithesis of high-end video-game verisimilitude: it leaves blanks the reader fills, showing how often we fill things in.
claims.source: Stephanie Burt, review of John Plotz, Ursula Le Guin's Earthsea (OUP 2023), Strange Horizons
claims.quote: the antithesis of the well-rendered verisimilitude

claims.claim: Plotz compares Le Guin's clear, spare prose to Willa Cather's.
claims.source: Stephanie Burt on Plotz (Strange Horizons)

claims.claim: Burt: the narration invites readers in and holds them back, reminding them they are hearing a story and making them co-creators, collaborators, listeners as if to an oral tale.
claims.source: Stephanie Burt (Strange Horizons)
claims.quote: co-creators, collaborators, listeners, as if to an oral tale

claims.claim: Burt names the clear, patient prose and its love for calm, open space, sky and sea, and likens the listening-and-waiting mode to Paradise Regained.
claims.source: Stephanie Burt (Strange Horizons)
claims.quote: clear, patient

claims.claim: Tearle credits Le Guin with picking up the right word on the end of her pen; Plotz devotes a chapter to her use of language and naming and to the careful, deliberate nature of her prose.
claims.source: Oliver Tearle, review of Plotz (Interesting Literature)
claims.quote: the careful and deliberate nature of her prose

claims.claim: Le Guin reads the fundamental rhythm of LOTR as two beats — stress and release, inbreath and outbreath, a heartbeat — irreducibly simple yet capable of endless variation.
claims.source: Kate Nepveu, LotR re-read: Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (summary of the 2001 essay)
claims.quote: Stress, release. Inbreath, outbreath. A heartbeat.

claims.claim: She lists pulsing pairs (darkness/daylight, confusion/clarity, trap/freedom) and insists they are not simple binary flips; each yang contains its yin.
claims.source: Kate Nepveu, LotR re-read: Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (summary of the 2001 essay)
claims.quote: are not simple binary flips

claims.claim: The narrative follows a physical gait — one, two, left, right, on foot from the Shire to the Mountain and back.
claims.source: Kate Nepveu, LotR re-read: Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (summary of the 2001 essay)

claims.claim: She scans a chapter closely, hears its close 'like drumbeats', and recommends reading passages aloud.
claims.source: Kate Nepveu, LotR re-read: Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (summary of the 2001 essay)
claims.quote: like drumbeats

claims.claim: Le Guin (quoted) on Tolkien: even long sentences flow clearly and follow the breath, punctuation comes where you need to pause, cadences are graceful and inevitable.
claims.source: Vermont Softworks blog on 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: their flow is perfectly clear, and follows the breath

claims.feature: the writer must hear the prose
claims.claim: Le Guin infers from read-aloud ease that Tolkien must have heard what he wrote.
claims.source: Vermont Softworks blog (quoting Le Guin)
claims.quote: Tolkien must have heard what he wrote

claims.claim: The sound of the language is where it all begins; the test of a sentence is whether it sounds right.
claims.source: Literary Hub, 'A Writing Lesson from Ursula K. Le Guin' (excerpt from Steering the Craft)
claims.quote: The sound of the language is where it all begins.

claims.claim: The chief duty of a narrative sentence is to lead to the next; pace and movement depend on rhythm you can only control by hearing it.
claims.source: Literary Hub, 'A Writing Lesson from Ursula K. Le Guin' (excerpt from Steering the Craft)
claims.quote: duty of a narrative sentence is to lead to the next

claims.claim: Writers need a mind's ear; dull, choppy, droning, jerky, feeble are faults of sound, lively, flowing, strong, beautiful its virtues.
claims.source: Literary Hub, 'A Writing Lesson from Ursula K. Le Guin' (excerpt from Steering the Craft)
claims.quote: a mind's ear

claims.claim: Prose's sound effects are subtle and always irregular (unlike verse); onomatopoeia, alliteration, repetition and dialect cadences are the tools, and changing sentence rhythms can express emotion.
claims.source: Literary Hub, 'A Writing Lesson from Ursula K. Le Guin' (excerpt from Steering the Craft)

claims.claim: The father tongue's essential gesture is not reasoning but distancing — one-way speech that expects no answer and 'only lectures'.
claims.source: Le Guin, Bryn Mawr Commencement Address (1986), text at Serendip
claims.quote: not reasoning but distancing

claims.claim: The mother tongue is conversation, language as relation whose power is in binding not dividing.
claims.source: Le Guin, Bryn Mawr Commencement Address (1986), text at Serendip
claims.quote: Expects an answer. It is conversation

claims.claim: The mother tongue is always on the verge of silence and often on the verge of song.
claims.source: Le Guin, Bryn Mawr Commencement Address (1986), text at Serendip
claims.quote: on the verge of silence and often on the verge of song

claims.claim: The third, native tongue of art welds the public father tongue and private mother tongue back together.
claims.source: Le Guin, Bryn Mawr Commencement Address (1986), text at Serendip
claims.quote: wedding and welding back together

claims.claim: Newell's MA thesis argues that the structuralist view of language revealed in the Earthsea Cycle underlies its depiction of power and balance.
claims.source: Daniel Newell, 'The Mother Tongue in a World of Sons: Language and Power in The Earthsea Cycle' (MA thesis, Liberty University 2010) — abstract
claims.quote: The structuralist view of language

claims.claim: A peer-reviewed article frames Earthsea's wizards' language as 'doing things with words' — speech-act power crossed with gender.
claims.source: Crossref record: Comoletti & Drout, 'How They Do Things with Words…', Children's Literature 29 (2001): 113–141, DOI 10.1353/chl.0.0786

claims.claim: A 1992 Extrapolation article treats rhythm as a narrative technique operating 'beyond words' in The Left Hand of Darkness.
claims.source: Crossref record: Nora Barry & Mary Prescott, 'Beyond Words: The Impact of Rhythm as Narrative Technique in The Left Hand of Darkness', Extrapolation 33.2 (1992): 154–165, DOI 10.3828/extr.1992.33.2.154

claims.feature: scholarly focus: voice and rhythm, not lexis
claims.claim: Weyant's secondary bibliography shows the style-adjacent scholarship clusters on narrative voice and structure (Adams 1991; Jose 1991; Castleman 2020), rhythm (Barry & Prescott 1992), and the 'language of realism' in terrain (Pegg 1995) — no stylometric or corpus study is listed.
claims.source: Curtis Weyant, The Left Hand of Darkness: Secondary Bibliography

claims.claim: David Mitchell (quoted on the official site) says the book reads like the retelling of a tale first told centuries ago.
claims.source: ursulakleguin.com, The Books of Earthsea page (quoting Mitchell)
claims.quote: reads like the retelling of a tale first told centuries ago

claims.claim: Steering the Craft insists the writer needs grammatical terms to say what is wrong or right in a sentence, likening the untooled writer to a carpenter who cannot tell a hammer from a screwdriver.
claims.source: ursulakleguin.com, Steering the Craft page
claims.quote: like a carpenter who doesn't know a hammer from a screwdriver

claims.claim: The second trilogy 'sees exactly the same world with different eyes', expanding rather than retracting the earlier books.
claims.source: Sharada Bhanu, 'Tehanu: A Return to the Source' (ursulakleguin.com)
claims.quote: sees exactly the same world with different eyes

0.trueWording: The style, of course, is the book.
0.note: p.9 verbatim; all limbs on page: 'as if it were an ingredient of a book... something added onto the book'; 'If you remove the style, all you have left is a synopsis of the plot'; 'partly true of history; largely true of fiction; and absolutely true of fantasy.'

1.trueWording: A plain language is the noblest of all.
1.note: p.8 verbatim, followed by 'It is also the most difficult.' Limbs on page: 'Most epics are in straightforward language... They retain the directness of their oral forebears'; 'The Mabinogian and the Norse sagas are as plainspoken as they could well be.' Context is explicitly heroic fantasy: 'We are discussing a modern descendant of the epic.' (Essay spells it 'Mabinogian'.)

2.trueWording: It is a fake plainness. It is not really simple, but flat.
2.note: p.8 verbatim. Limbs on page: 'It is not really clear, but inexact. Its directness is specious'; 'It is journalistic prose. In journalism, the suppression of the author's personality and sensibility is deliberate'; 'A language intended to express the immediate and the trivial is applied to the remote and the elemental.' Commercial framing on same page: 'Fantasy is selling well, so let's all grind out a fantasy. The Old Baloney Factory.'

3.trueWording: the scenery is cardboard, or plastic
3.note: p.8 verbatim, inside 'Its sensory cues--extremely important in imaginative writing--are vague and generalized; the rocks, the wind, the trees are not there, are not felt; the scenery is cardboard, or plastic.' Every limb, including the parenthetical quotation, is on the page.

4.trueWording: It's a high wire: one slip spoils all.
4.note: p.6 verbatim, preceded by 'The archaic manner is indeed a perfect distancer, but you have to do it perfectly.' The four failure markers are all on pp.5-6: botched thee/thou verbs ('Whithersoever thou goest there also I goest'), the subjunctive ('All the was's turn into were's'), 'Mayhap', and 'the final test, the infallible touchstone of the seventh-rate: Ichor.' Minor: the word 'touchstone' is applied literally only to ichor; the other three are catalogued as novice traps, not called touchstones.

5.trueWording: And it contains no archaisms at all.
5.note: p.7 verbatim, closing the Vance paragraph after 'It is an achieved style.' Limbs on page: 'The conversation of his characters is aloof and restrained, very like his own narrative prose'; p.8 opens 'After all, archaisms are not essential'; the distancing purpose is stated on p.5 ('what is wanted in fantasy is a distancing from the ordinary'). 'Consistent' is carried by 'very like his own narrative prose' and 'he never shows a tin ear for tone' -- the phrase 'His tone is perfectly consistent' belongs to Cabell, not Vance.

6.trueWording: the characters lose coherence in my mind
6.note: p.7 verbatim, inside 'I am jerked back and forth between Elland [sic: Elfland] and Poughkeepsie; the characters lose coherence in my mind, and I lose confidence in them.' Limbs on page: 'Fritz Leiber and Roger Zelazny... they alternate the two styles. When humor is intended the characters talk colloquial American English, or even slang, and at earnest moments they revert to old formal usages.'

7.note: p.4 verbatim, followed by 'It does so whether the speaker or the author knows it or not.' Limbs on page: 'When I hear a man say, "I could have told you that at Cardosa"... He is the kind who says, "I told you so." Nobody who says, "I told you so" has ever been, or will ever be, a hero'; and 'You could not pull the trick on them that I pulled on Morgan and Nigel--not unless you changed half the words in every sentence. You could not possibly mistake them for anyone on Capitol Hill' (the trick being the four-word change of p.2).

8.trueWording: Its outstanding virtue is its flexibility, its variety.
8.note: p.8 verbatim. Limbs on page: 'Tolkien writes a plain, clear English'; 'It ranges easily from the commonplace to the stately, and can slide into metrical poetry, as in the Tom Bombadil episode, without the careless readers even noticing'; 'Tolkien's vocabulary is not striking; he has no ichor; everything is direct, concrete, and simple.'

9.trueWording: the movement of the syntax, and the rhythm of the sentences
9.note: p.6 verbatim. Limbs on page: 'That prose, in spite of or because of its archaisms, is good prose: exact, clear, powerful. Visually it is precise and vivid; musically--that is, in the sound of the words, the movement of the syntax, and the rhythm of the sentences--it is subtle and very strong. Nothing in it is faked or blurred.' The subject is Eddison's Worm Ouroboros passage.

10.note: p.10 verbatim. Limbs on page: 'There is no borrowed reality of history, or current events... to disguise flaws and failures of creation'; 'There is only a construct built in a void, with every joint and seam and nail exposed'; 'The only voice that speaks there is the creator's voice.'

11.trueWording: a lot of elaborate made-up names, some vague descriptions of gorgeous cities and unmentionable dooms, and a great many sentences beginning with "And."
11.note: p.5 quotation is verbatim and the three diagnostic items are exactly on the page. The essay names the King James Bible only as a formative influence on Dunsany's OWN prose ('one of the profoundest formative influences on Dunsany's prose'; imitators are out of reach unless 'brought up from the cradle on the grand sonorities of Genesis and Ecclesiastes'); it never attributes the imitators' 'And' sentences to biblical cadence, and never frames them as costume. That reading is a defensible inference, not the page's statement.
11.unsupportedLimb: biblical cadence worn as costume -- the essay ties the KJV to Dunsany himself, never says imitators wear biblical cadence as costume

12.trueWording: with what importance they invest these trivial acts
12.note: p.4 verbatim, inside 'But with what importance they invest these trivial acts, what emotion, what vitality!' Limbs on page: 'Nothing is really going on, in those first two passages: in one case they're reading a book, in the other they're dividing a cold leg of rabbit' -- and the first two passages are footnoted to Eddison (Worm Ouroboros) and Kenneth Morris (Book of the Three Dragons). 'Elevation lies in the speech, not the event' is the paragraph's own argument ('All of them are heroic, eloquent, passionate... greatness of soul shows when a man speaks').

13.trueWording: an English extraordinary for its simple timelessness
13.note: p.4 verbatim. Limbs on page: 'It has sobriety, wit, and force. It is the language of men of character.' The third passage is footnoted to Tolkien, Fellowship of the Ring (Aragorn, Boromir, Elrond). 'Rather than mannered archaism' is carried by the contrast drawn in the same sentence: 'the speakers are quieter, and use a less extraordinary English' than the Eddison and Morris passages.

14.trueWording: fantastic creation should reach to the very words and grammar
14.note: Wikipedia article fetched raw (wikitext via ?action=raw and rendered HTML, oldid 1352490882, last edited 4 May 2026). Verbatim: 'In her argument that fantastic creation should reach to the very words and grammar in fantasy writers, she holds up Lord Dunsany, E. R. Eddison...' Beagle limb verbatim: 'The novelist Peter S. Beagle called it "the definitive piece on fantasy, and on why simply sprinkling goblins, magic swords, and assorted thees and thous through your story will not get you a step closer to that vast and beautiful realm."' Note the page frames the work as a 1972 speech published 1973.

15.trueWording: holds up those seven writers as successful examples
15.note: Raw wikitext + rendered plaintext (Special:Export + action=query prop=extracts). Page: 'In her argument that fantastic creation should reach to the very words and grammar in fantasy writers, she holds up Lord Dunsany, E. R. Eddison, Kenneth Morris, J. R. R. Tolkien, James Branch Cabell, Evangeline Walton, and Jack Vance as successful examples.' All seven names match in order; the claim's gloss 'models of style that fits its world' is a paraphrase of 'fantastic creation should reach to the very words and grammar', hence SUBSTANCE not VERBATIM (claim carried no quote).

16.trueWording: because there is no known framework for the reader's mind to rest upon
16.note: Raw wikitext, Style-and-mood section: 'Le Guin herself said that in fantasy it was necessary to be clear and direct with language, because there is no known framework for the reader's mind to rest upon.' Quoted fragment is word-for-word; both limbs (clear and direct; no framework for the reader) supported. Cited to Slusser 1976 pp.32-35.

17.trueWording: makes the narrator seem sympathetic, does not distance his thoughts
17.note: Raw wikitext: 'This narrative technique, which Cadden characterizes as "free indirect discourse", makes the narrator of the book seem sympathetic to the protagonist, and does not distance his thoughts from the reader.' Quote verbatim; 'Mike Cadden' confirmed elsewhere on the same page ('Scholar Mike Cadden'); sympathy limb supported; blending of protagonist feelings with narration supported only loosely ('does not distance his thoughts from the reader') and stated squarely on the SEPARATE Ursula K. Le Guin article, not this one. Nothing on this page says anything about narrative flexibility.
17.unsupportedLimb: 'while keeping narrative flexibility' - the cited page never claims the technique preserves flexibility

18.trueWording: the narration switches from looking ahead into Ged's future
18.note: Raw wikitext: 'The story often appears to assume that readers are familiar with the geography and history of Earthsea, a technique which allowed Le Guin to avoid exposition ... In keeping with the notion of an epic, the narration switches from looking ahead into Ged's future and looking back into the past of Earthsea.' Quote verbatim; all limbs present. Minor hedge: the page says 'often appears to assume' where the claim asserts it flatly.

19.trueWording: gives Le Guin's world the mysterious depths of Tolkien's, but without his tiresome back-stories and versifying
19.note: Raw wikitext: 'a reviewer wrote that this method "gives Le Guin's world the mysterious depths of Tolkien's, but without his tiresome back-stories and versifying"', ref name='Craig 2003' (Amanda Craig, The Guardian, 24 Sep 2003). Quote verbatim; 'a reviewer' and the crediting of the no-exposition method both supported.

20.trueWording: Slusser described the mood of the novel as "strange and dreamlike"
20.note: Raw wikitext: 'Slusser described the mood of the novel as "strange and dreamlike", fluctuating between objective reality and the thoughts in Ged's mind'. Quote verbatim; the fluctuation limb is present word for word; 'George Slusser' is given in full earlier in the same section, cited to Slusser 1976 pp.35-38.

21.trueWording: in prose as taut and clean as a ship's sail
21.note: Raw wikitext, Reception: 'a review in The Guardian by author and journalist Amanda Craig said it was "The most thrilling, wise and beautiful children's novel ever, [written] in prose as taut and clean as a ship's sail."' Quote verbatim; Craig and The Guardian both named on the page.

22.trueWording: Slusser: "work of high style and imagination"; "genuine epic vision" cited to Cadden
22.note: Raw wikitext: 'Slusser described the Earthsea cycle as a "work of high style and imagination",{{sfn|Slusser|1976|pp=32-35}} and the original trilogy of books a product of "genuine epic vision".{{sfn|Cadden|2005|p=86}}' The quoted limb is verbatim and is Slusser 1976. The second limb is footnoted to Cadden 2005 and its object is the original trilogy, not the cycle.
22.unsupportedLimb: 'the Earthsea cycle ... with genuine epic vision' per Slusser 1976 - the page applies 'genuine epic vision' to the original trilogy and footnotes it to Cadden 2005

23.trueWording: Every word was exactly in place and every sentence or line had resonance
23.note: Raw wikitext: 'literary critic Harold Bloom described Le Guin as an "exquisite stylist", saying that in her writing, "Every word was exactly in place and every sentence or line had resonance".' Quote verbatim; 'exquisite stylist', exact placement and resonance all present.

24.trueWording: described her as using "a lean but lyrical style" to explore issues of moral relevance
24.note: Raw wikitext: 'The New York Times described her as using "a lean but lyrical style" to explore issues of moral relevance.' Quote verbatim; the moral-issues limb is supported as 'issues of moral relevance'. The page attributes the style to her writing rather than the word 'prose', a wording difference only.

25.trueWording: Her prose, according to Zadie Smith, was "as elegant and beautiful as any written in the twentieth century"
25.note: Raw wikitext: exact sentence present, ref 'Fellow Writers' (Library of America, 26 Jan 2018). Quote verbatim; every limb supported.

26.trueWording: personal narration, diary extracts, Gethenian myths, and ethnological reports; "distinctly post-modern"
26.note: Raw wikitext, same paragraph: 'The heterogeneous structure of The Left Hand of Darkness, described as "distinctly post-modern", was unusual for the time of its publication' and '... the material, consisting of personal narration, diary extracts, Gethenian myths, and ethnological reports.' Quote verbatim; all four components present.

27.trueWording: described by Bloom as "precise, dialectical-always evocative in its restrained pathos"
27.note: Raw wikitext has 'restrained [[pathos]]' (wikilink), so the quote was confirmed against the RENDERED plaintext extract via action=query&prop=extracts&explaintext, where the exact string 'precise, dialectical—always evocative in its restrained pathos' is present (em dash, as in the claim). Attributed to Bloom 1987 and applied to Le Guin's writing style in this novel.

28.trueWording: tales immediately precede chapters describing Ai's similar experience; explain culture and philosophy
28.note: Raw wikitext: 'The myths and legends serve to explain specific features about Gethenian culture, as well as larger philosophical aspects of society. Many of the tales used in the novel immediately precede chapters describing Ai's experience with a similar situation.' Claim carried no quote and is a paraphrase; both limbs supported. Page hedges with 'Many of the tales' where the claim generalises.

29.trueWording: first-person narration reflects his slowly developing view; White: initially confusing to reviewers
29.note: Raw wikitext: 'Ai's first-person narration reflects his slowly developing view, and the reader's knowledge and understanding of the Gethens evolves with Ai's awareness. He begins in naivety, gradually discovering his profound errors in judgement.' And: 'In 1999, literary scholar Donna White wrote that the unorthodox structure of the novel made it initially confusing to reviewers, before it was interpreted as an attempt to follow the trajectory of Ai's changing views.' Both limbs supported; claim carried no quote, hence SUBSTANCE.

30.note: Live en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tombs_of_Atuan (rendered page + Special:Export wikitext). Quote verbatim: 'making the narrator seem sympathetic to the characters' (cited Cadden 2005 p.92). Both other limbs verbatim too: 'In The Tombs of Atuan, much of the story is told from Tenar's perspective; for instance, the reader sees Tenar's fear of the undertomb through her own eyes, creating an empathy for her' (Cadden 2005 p.94). Minor scope point, not a limb of the claim: the page attributes free indirect discourse to the Earthsea trilogy generally, not to Tombs specifically.

31.note: Same page. Verbatim: 'Science fiction writer Jo Walton said that it was a "beautifully written" book. She went on to write that a "lesser writer" would have ended the novel after the earthquake and the collapse of the Tombs, but that the last section of the story, about Ged and Tenar's travel, "do a lot to ground it", making it "solid and well rooted as ever".' Every limb (Walton, final travel section, grounding, after the earthquake) supported.

32.note: Live en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tehanu. Verbatim: Kirkus Reviews '...even young readers will be beguiled by the flawless, poetic prose, the philosophy expressed in thoughtful, potent metaphor, and the consummately imagined world' (ref Kirkus, January 15, 1990). Both limbs — flawless poetic prose and thoughtful, potent metaphor — supported.

33.note: Same page. Verbatim: Dirda in The Washington Post — Tehanu is 'less sheerly exciting' but perhaps 'the most moving'; the book gives the Earthsea themes 'a darker, more realistic edge'; and 'Further, Tehanu presents the world from a woman's point of view...' all carrying ref name 'Dirda 1990' ('The Twilight of an Age of Magic', February 25, 1990). All four limbs supported, and the claim correctly preserves Dirda's 'perhaps'.

34.note: Same page. Verbatim: 'Jo Walton finds Tehanu "problematic", writing that it is "a restless book with very strange pacing", but that it is surprising that it "works as well as it does", given the competing demands of "the force of story" - plot, action - and Le Guin's evident intention to place "women's domestic lives" at the novel's centre.' The 'torn between plot and women's domestic lives' limb is supported by that competing-demands sentence; note the page frames it as competing demands the book nonetheless survives, not as a failure.

35.note: NEA PDF fetched live (HTTP 200, 515,637 bytes, 12 pages), text extracted with pypdf. Printed page 4, 'The Language of Fantasy': 'Throughout A Wizard of Earthsea Le Guin's language is plain, strong, and exact; her tone grave and slightly formal; and the rhythm of her sentences carefully balanced and musical.' Quote verbatim; both limbs (diction and tone) supported. Page attribution p.4 is correct.

36.note: Same sentence, same printed page 4: 'the rhythm of her sentences carefully balanced and musical'. Quote verbatim, limb supported. Page attribution p.4 correct.

37.note: Printed page 4, immediately following: 'Note the occasional touches of alliteration and assonance-reminiscent of Old English verse-in such phrases as this: "Forest rises ridge behind ridge to the stone and snow of the heights."' Quote verbatim; the alliteration/assonance limb and the cited example sentence both verbatim. Page attribution p.4 correct.

38.note: Printed page 5, 'An Interview with Ursula K. Le Guin': header reads 'On January 7, 2008, Dan Stone of the National Endowment for the Arts interviewed Ursula K. Le Guin at her home in Oregon' - the 2008 limb is confirmed on the page. UKL: 'What a wizard does is like what a writer does. He or she is making things out of words and making things happen with words.' Quote verbatim; every limb supported. Page attribution p.5 correct (the answer sits on p.5, the interview continues onto p.6).

39.note: Printed page 9, 'Le Guin and Her Other Works': 'Perhaps the best-known and most taught of all modern science fiction novels, The Left Hand of Darkness is written in a tone even more gravely austere than A Wizard of Earthsea.' Quote verbatim; both limbs supported. Page attribution p.9 correct.

40.note: Printed page 10, Discussion Questions, question 4: 'The language of A Wizard of Earthsea is often quietly poetic. Comment on three sentences that you find particularly beautiful or moving.' Quote verbatim, and it is indeed a discussion question. Page attribution p.10 correct.

41.note: Printed page 3, 'Introduction to the Book': 'The book's elegant diction, geographical sweep, and mounting suspense are quite irresistible.' Quote verbatim, all three limbs supported, and it does sit under the heading 'Introduction to the Book'. Page attribution p.3 correct.

42.trueWording: Page credits 'taut and clean' to The Guardian, unnamed
42.unsupportedLimb: the attribution of 'taut and clean as a ship's sail' to Craig - the page credits that quotation only to 'The Guardian' and the string 'Craig' does not occur anywhere in the page's HTML (case-insensitive grep of the raw source returned zero hits)
42.note: Live arts.gov page fetched (HTTP 200, 74,952 bytes). Both quotations ARE on the page: the Overview carries '...it is written in prose as taut and clean as a ship's sail.... It poses the deep questions about life, death, power and responsibility that children need answering' (The Guardian), and an accordion panel reproduces the guide's 'Language of Fantasy' text verbatim including 'plain, strong, and exact'. So the 'repeats the guide's characterization' limb and the 'pairs it with' limb are both supported; only the Craig attribution is absent from the page. (Amanda Craig did write the Guardian review, but that cannot be verified from this URL, which is what was cited.)

43.note: Live sf-encyclopedia.com/entry/le_guin_ursula_k fetched (HTTP 200, 101,578 bytes). Verbatim: 'The initial Earthsea trilogy, austere but vivid, is a major work whose appeal goes far beyond the Young Adult audience at whom in the first instance it was aimed'. Quote verbatim; all three limbs (austere but vivid, major work, reaching beyond the Young Adult audience) supported.

44.note: Same page: 'A grave joyfulness pervades the trilogy, which is perhaps more maturely thoughtful (while remaining exciting) than the comparable Narnia series of C S Lewis.' Quote verbatim and every limb present. FLAG for downstream use: the claim drops SFE's hedge 'perhaps' - the source qualifies the Narnia comparison, so restore 'perhaps' if the sentence is quoted as SFE's position.
